analogy.p: Think of geographical skills as a toolkit in a workshop. A map is the blueprint, graphs are the measuring tapes and gauges, and statistics are the calculators that turn raw measurements into a verdict. Just as a carpenter picks the right tool for each job, you pick the right graph or statistic for the data. The analogy breaks down because the tools in a workshop do not change the material they measure, whereas a poorly chosen graph or an average distorted by an anomaly can mislead you.

bullets: **Cartographic skills**: atlas, Ordnance Survey (OS) and other maps; scale, distance, direction, grid references, relief, contours and map symbols.
**Graphical skills**: select, draw, complete, interpret and describe a range of graphs and charts.
**Numerical skills**: percentages, ratios, proportions, fractions, simple calculations and unit conversions.
**Statistical skills**: mean, median, mode, range, interquartile range, and understanding of sampling.
**ICT and GIS**: use of digital maps, satellite images and geographical information systems.
**Literacy and communication**: use of geographical terminology and extended writing.
core.p: The AQA specification lists geographical skills that students must be able to use throughout the course, in physical, human and fieldwork contexts. They are grouped as **cartographic skills** (maps), **graphical skills** (charts and graphs), **numerical skills**, **statistical skills**, **ICT and GIS skills**, and **literacy skills**. Examiners can test them on any paper and with any topic, so they are one of the most reliable ways to earn marks. In Paper 3 especially, you must apply them to unfamiliar maps, graphs and data.

bullets: **Choropleth**: areas shaded by value (darker shading = higher value); good for comparing regions, but hides variation within each area.
**Isoline**: lines joining places of equal value (contours, isobars, isotherms); close lines show rapid change.
**Dot map**: each dot represents a quantity; shows distribution and clustering.
**Proportional symbols**: size of circle or bar shows quantity, e.g. city populations.
**Flow lines**: width of arrow shows volume of movement, e.g. migration or trade.
**Atlas maps**: show general location, physical and human features; small scale.
**Sketch maps and annotated maps**: used in fieldwork to record key features.
core.h: Types of map and when to use them
core.p: Different maps show different kinds of information. A **topographic map** (such as an OS map) shows physical and human features like roads, rivers and relief. A **thematic map** shows a single theme such as population density or rainfall. Choosing the right type matters: a **choropleth** map uses shading for areas, an **isoline** map joins points of equal value, a **dot map** shows distribution, **proportional symbols** vary in size by quantity and **flow lines** show movement. You must be able to interpret each and say what pattern it shows.

bullets: **1:50 000**: 1 cm on the map = 0.5 km on the ground; 2 cm = 1 km.
Distance = **map distance x scale denominator**, then convert units (100 000 cm = 1 km).
**Straight-line distance** is measured with a ruler; **route distance** along a road or river uses string.
A **large-scale map shows more detail**; a **small-scale map shows a bigger area**.
Always state **units** (m or km) in your answer.
core.p: Scale tells you how distances on a map relate to real distances. A **representative fraction** such as 1:50 000 means that 1 unit on the map equals 50 000 of the same unit on the ground, so 1 cm on the map is 50 000 cm, which is 500 m, on the ground. OS Explorer maps are 1:25 000 and Landranger maps are 1:50 000. A **large-scale** map (such as 1:25 000) shows a small area in detail; a **small-scale** map (such as 1:1 000 000) shows a large area in less detail. For curved routes, measure along the route with string or a strip of paper, then compare with the scale line.

bullets: North = 0 degrees (360), East = 90, South = 180, West = 270.
Intermediate points: **NE = 45, SE = 135, SW = 225, NW = 315** degrees.
Direction **from A to B**: start at A, face B.
To describe a feature's position, use **'to the north-east of the village'** rather than 'top right'.
Check the **north arrow**; some maps are not orientated with north at the top.
Use a **protractor** from a north line for bearings when asked.
core.p: On most maps, north is at the top. Directions use the eight points of the compass (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW), and **bearings** use degrees clockwise from north (0 to 360). Examiners usually ask for a compass direction such as 'south-west'. When asked for the direction from A to B, begin at A and look towards B, not the other way around, which is a common error.

bullets: Remember: **'along the corridor, then up the stairs'** (eastings first, then northings).
**4-figure** reference: easting + northing of the **bottom-left corner** of the square, e.g. 3620.
**6-figure** reference: three digits for easting (36 + 6 tenths = 366) and three for northing (20 + 4 tenths = 204), giving 366204.
Always give the numbers in the **correct order** and keep the leading zeros.
To find a feature from a grid reference, **go along first, then up**.
Check the **grid square numbers** on the edge, not the numbers inside the map.
In the exam, you may be asked to **give the grid reference** of a named feature or to **identify the feature** at a reference.
core.p: The OS grid divides a map into squares one kilometre wide. The **eastings** (vertical lines) are numbered along the bottom and top, and the **northings** (horizontal lines) are numbered up the sides. A **four-figure grid reference** identifies a whole square: read the easting of the line on the left of the square, then the northing of the line below it. A **six-figure reference** locates a point within the square by dividing it into tenths: add one digit after the easting for how many tenths across, and one after the northing for how many tenths up.

bullets: **Closely spaced contours** = steep slope; **widely spaced** = gentle slope.
**Concentric rings** with increasing numbers = hill or summit.
**'V' shapes pointing to higher ground** = river valley; V shapes pointing to lower ground = spur or ridge.
**Spot heights** (black dot with number) and **trig points** (blue triangle) show exact heights.
**Cross-sections** are drawn by marking heights along a line and joining them; label the axes and keep the vertical scale sensible.
**Vertical exaggeration** makes slopes look steeper than they are.
Use contours to explain **land use** (steep slopes often forest or moorland, flat land farming or settlement).
core.p: **Contours** are lines joining points of equal height above sea level. On OS maps they are drawn in brown, usually at 10 m intervals on 1:25 000 and 1:50 000 maps. The **spacing** of contours shows the steepness of the slope: closely spaced lines show a steep slope, widely spaced lines a gentle one. Contours also show shape: rings of closed contours form hills, 'V' shapes pointing uphill show valleys and 'V' shapes pointing downhill show spurs. Spot heights and triangulation pillars give exact heights.

bullets: **Nucleated**: buildings clustered around a centre, often at a crossroads.
**Linear**: buildings in a line along a road, river or valley.
**Dispersed**: isolated farms and houses spread across the area.
**Site**: the actual land on which the settlement is built; **situation**: its position in relation to surrounding features.
Use the **key** to identify land use, transport, services and tourism features.
Use **grid references and place names** to support points.
Describe a pattern by **location, shape, and spacing**, not just 'there are lots of buildings'.
core.h: Map symbols, land use and settlement patterns
core.p: OS maps use symbols explained in the key, such as blue for water, green for woodland, black for roads and buildings, and brown for contours. You must be able to interpret land use and settlement patterns from a map. **Settlement shapes** are described as **nucleated** (clustered), **linear** (along a road or river) or **dispersed** (scattered). The site and situation of a settlement can be explained from map evidence (flat land, water, routes, relief). Marks are earned for using map evidence with grid references.

bullets: **Bar chart**: categories, e.g. land use types; bars separated; frequency or value on the y-axis.
**Histogram**: continuous data in classes of equal width; bars touch.
**Line graph**: change over time; plot points and join them with straight lines.
**Scatter graph**: two numerical variables; add a **line of best fit** to show correlation.
**Pie chart**: proportion of the whole (angle = percentage x 3.6).
**Divided bar graph**: shows how a total is divided; useful for comparing breakdowns.
Always add a **title**, **labelled axes with units**, and a **suitable scale** starting at zero where appropriate.
core.p: The graph you choose should suit the type of data and the message. **Bar charts** compare separate categories (with gaps between bars). **Histograms** show continuous data grouped into equal classes (no gaps). **Line graphs** show change over time or a continuous variable. **Scatter graphs** show whether two variables are related, with a line of best fit. **Pie charts** show proportions of a whole. **Pictograms** and **divided bars** show proportions or counts. Examiners often ask you to justify a choice, so state what the graph shows well.

bullets: **Population pyramid**: males on one side, females on the other, age bands on the vertical axis; wide base = high birth rate.
**Kite diagram**: shows change along a line such as a transect across sand dunes; symmetrical shapes centred on the line.
**Radial (radar) graph**: values plotted on axes radiating from the centre; shows direction or cyclical data.
**Triangular graph**: each corner represents 100% of one category; used for soil texture, employment sectors.
**Logarithmic scale**: each division is a multiple (x10) of the previous; useful for large ranges, e.g. earthquake energy.
**Cumulative frequency graph** and **dispersion graph** show distribution and spread.
For all graphs: **read the key and axes carefully** before describing.
core.h: Specialist graphs: population pyramids, kite, radial and triangular
core.p: The AQA specification includes several specialist graph types. A **population pyramid** shows the age and sex structure of a population as back-to-back horizontal bars. A **kite diagram** shows distribution of a species or a feature along a transect, with width representing frequency. A **radial graph** (radar graph) plots data in a circular layout, such as wind direction or pedestrian flow by direction. A **triangular graph** shows data with three categories that add up to 100%. A **logarithmic scale** is used when data cover a very large range, with each step representing a multiple of ten.

bullets: **General trend**: 'rises steadily', 'falls sharply', 'fluctuates', 'peaks at'.
**Quote data**: 'increases from 12 to 48 between 2000 and 2020'.
**Calculate a change**: a difference or percentage, e.g. +36 or +300%.
**Anomalies**: values that break the pattern; give the value and where.
**Correlation**: positive (both rise), negative (one rises, other falls), or none.
**Correlation is not causation**: a link does not prove one variable causes the other.
Always **read the axis scale** carefully: look out for broken axes, different units and non-zero starting points.
core.p: Describing a graph means stating **what the data show using figures**, while explaining means saying **why**. A high-scoring description follows a pattern: general trend, supporting data, then exceptions. Quote values with units, give start and end values, use comparison words and calculate changes where helpful. Interpretation also includes spotting **anomalies**, **correlation** (positive, negative, or none) and **limitations** such as misleading scales or small samples.

bullets: **Percentage of a total** = (part / total) x 100.
**Percentage change** = (new - old) / old x 100; e.g. 12 500 to 15 000 = 2 500 / 12 500 x 100 = **20% increase**.
**Ratio**: simplify, e.g. 30 men : 20 women = 3 : 2.
**Fractions and proportions**: 'three-quarters', 0.75 and 75% are equivalent.
**Rates**: per 1000 or per 100 000 (e.g. birth rate = births / population x 1000).
**Unit conversions**: 1 km = 1000 m; 1 m = 100 cm; 1 hectare = 10 000 m squared.
Give answers to a **sensible number of significant figures or decimal places**, and always include **units**.
core.h: Numerical skills: percentages, ratios and proportions
core.p: Numerical skills are tested using geographical data such as population, rainfall, GDP and fieldwork counts. You must be able to calculate **percentages**, **percentage change**, **ratios**, **fractions** and **simple averages**, and to convert units. The **percentage change** formula is (new - old) / old x 100. Showing working scores method marks even if the final answer is wrong. For ratio questions, simplify by dividing by a common factor.

bullets: **Mean** = total of all values / number of values; sensitive to **anomalies**.
**Median**: order the data first; with an even number of values take the mean of the middle two.
**Mode**: the most common value (a set can have more than one mode).
**Range** = highest - lowest.
**Lower quartile (Q1)**: median of the lower half; **upper quartile (Q3)**: median of the upper half; **IQR = Q3 - Q1**.
A **small IQR** means data are consistent; a **large IQR** means values are spread out.
Worked example: data 4, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 31 give median 15, Q1 = 8, Q3 = 24.5, IQR = 16.5, range = 27, mean = 16.1.
core.p: The key statistics are the **mean**, **median**, **mode**, **range** and **interquartile range** (IQR). The **mean** is the sum divided by the number of values. The **median** is the middle value of ordered data. The **mode** is the most frequent value. The **range** is largest minus smallest and shows total spread but is distorted by extreme values. The **IQR** is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile and shows the spread of the middle 50%, so it is not affected by anomalies. Comparing the median and IQR of two data sets is a powerful way to describe differences.

bullets: **Random**: use random numbers; avoids bias but may miss areas.
**Systematic**: every nth person or site; even coverage.
**Stratified**: sample sizes in proportion to sub-group size; most representative.
**Quantitative** data are numerical; **qualitative** data are descriptive, such as opinions.
**Primary** data are collected first-hand; **secondary** data come from other sources, such as census data.
**Bias**: tendency to favour some results; reduces validity.
Comment on **sample size**: larger samples are more reliable but take more time.
core.h: Sampling, data types and data quality
core.p: Geographers rarely study everything, so they use **sampling**. **Random sampling** gives every item an equal chance, **systematic sampling** selects at regular intervals and **stratified sampling** ensures groups are represented proportionately. You should recognise **primary** and **secondary** data, **quantitative** and **qualitative** data, and understand that the quality of conclusions depends on sample size and bias. A sample that is too small or unrepresentative can produce misleading results, so you should comment on this when interpreting data.

bullets: **GIS layers**: e.g. relief, rivers, land use, population; combine layers to find relationships.
**Satellite imagery**: shows large areas and change over time, e.g. deforestation or flooding.
**Aerial photographs**: oblique or vertical images show land use and settlement patterns.
**Spreadsheets**: calculate means, percentages and draw graphs quickly and accurately.
**GPS**: records precise locations during fieldwork.
**Limitations**: data may be out of date, low resolution, or need specialist software.
Be ready to suggest **how GIS could be used** to investigate a geographical issue.
core.p: Geographers use digital technologies to collect, store, analyse and present data. **GIS** (geographical information systems) store data in layers that can be switched on and off, helping to spot patterns and relationships (for example flood risk overlaid on land use). **Satellite images** and **aerial photographs** show land use and change over time, and **remote sensing** gathers data from a distance. Digital tools such as spreadsheets can calculate statistics and draw graphs, while online maps give up-to-date information.

bullets: **Rivers**: cross-sections, long profiles and hydrographs use line and bar graphs.
**Coasts**: OS map interpretation of landforms and management.
**Urban**: population pyramids, choropleth maps and land use maps.
**Development**: scatter graphs of GDP and life expectancy, triangular graphs of employment.
**Fieldwork**: choosing graphs, calculating statistics and interpreting patterns.
**Paper 3**: unfamiliar map and data interpretation in issue evaluation.
core.p: Skills are not a separate topic; they are used everywhere. Hazard maps and isoline maps of pressure appear in weather and climate, population pyramids in the urban and development topics, flow lines in migration and trade, hydrographs in rivers, and OS map interpretation in coasts, rivers and settlement. In fieldwork, the same techniques are used to present and analyse data, and in the pre-release for Paper 3 they are used to evaluate evidence. Practising skills across topics is the quickest way to raise your marks.

exam: Skills questions often carry **1 to 4 marks**; a calculation with working earns **method marks** even if the final answer is wrong.
For **'Calculate'**, show the **formula, substitution and answer with units**.
For **'Describe'**, give the **general trend, quote data, and mention any anomaly**.
For **'Suggest a suitable graph'**, name the graph and **justify it** by data type (e.g. 'a scatter graph because both variables are numerical and I want to show correlation').
For grid references, give **eastings first, then northings**, and use **6 figures** when asked for an exact point.
For scale questions, convert carefully: **cm to m to km**, and check your answer is sensible.
For contour questions, **use the spacing** to say steep or gentle and **quote heights**.
To complete a graph, use a **ruler, a sharp pencil, and plot exactly**; label axes and add a key if there is more than one data set.
For population pyramids, comment on **base width, top width, and male/female differences**.
When asked for the **IQR**, order the data and show **Q1, Q3 and the subtraction**.
Always check **axis scales and units** before describing a graph.
Use **map evidence** with grid references or place names to support answers on OS maps.

mistakes.r: Give the easting first (along) and then the northing (up).
mistakes.w: Giving the northing before the easting in a grid reference.

mistakes.r: Start at the first named point and face the second.
mistakes.w: Measuring direction from B to A instead of A to B.

mistakes.r: 1 cm is 50 000 cm, which is 500 m or 0.5 km.
Close contour lines show a steep slope; widely spaced lines show a gentle slope.
mistakes.w: Close contour lines show a gentle slope.

mistakes.r: Use histograms for continuous data (bars touch) and bar charts for categories (gaps).
mistakes.w: Using a bar chart for continuous data or a histogram for categories.

mistakes.r: Quote values with units, give a start and end figure and calculate a change.
mistakes.w: Describing a graph without any figures.

mistakes.r: The mean is affected by anomalies; the median or IQR may be more suitable when extreme values exist.
mistakes.w: Mean is always the best average.

mistakes.r: Order the data, find the median, then Q1 and Q3, then subtract.
mistakes.w: Calculating the IQR without ordering the data.

mistakes.r: Correlation shows a relationship but does not prove cause.
mistakes.w: Correlation proves one variable causes the other.

mistakes.r: Always write units (km, m, %, people per km squared) with the number.

summary: AQA GCSE Geography requires cartographic, graphical, numerical, statistical and digital skills that are tested across all three papers, including unfamiliar data on Paper 3. You must be able to read and use maps (scale, distance, direction, grid references, contours), choose, draw and interpret graphs, and calculate and use statistics such as the mean, median, mode, range, interquartile range, percentage change and ratios.

terms.d: The relationship between a distance on a map and the real distance on the ground.
A map that shows a small area in great detail, such as 1:25 000.
A map that shows a large area with less detail, such as an atlas map.
A line on a map joining points of equal height above sea level.
A set of numbers (eastings then northings) that locates a square or point on an OS map.
A vertical grid line; the number read along the bottom of an OS map.
A horizontal grid line; the number read up the side of an OS map.
A map in which areas are shaded according to the value of a variable.
A line on a map joining points of equal value.
A graph of continuous data grouped in classes, with bars that touch.
A graph that plots two variables to show whether they are correlated.
A graph showing the age and sex structure of a population.
The sum of all values divided by the number of values.
The middle value when data are arranged in order.
The value that occurs most often.
The difference between the largest and the smallest value.
The difference between the upper quartile and the lower quartile, showing the spread of the middle 50% of data.
A geographical information system that stores, analyses and displays spatial data in layers.
A value that does not fit the general pattern of the data.

worked.q: A point on an OS map is 0.7 of the way across and 0.3 of the way up the square whose bottom-left corner is at easting 41 and northing 87. (a) Give the four-figure and six-figure grid references. (b) The distance between two features is 4.6 cm on a 1:50 000 map. Calculate the real distance in km. (4 marks)
steps: Four-figure reference uses the bottom-left corner of the square: easting 41, northing 87, so 4187.
For the six-figure reference, add the tenths: easting 41 + 0.7 gives 417, northing 87 + 0.3 gives 873, so 417873.
Real distance = map distance x scale denominator = 4.6 x 50 000 = 230 000 cm.

worked.ans: The population increased by 20%. A choropleth map would use darker shading for areas with greater percentage increase, showing the spatial pattern of growth.
worked.q: The population of a town increased from 12 500 to 15 000 in ten years. Calculate the percentage change and describe what a choropleth map of population change would show. (3 marks)
steps: A choropleth shades areas by value, so towns with larger percentage increase would be darker, showing where growth is concentrated.
